orders.description: Appeal from the September 11, 2009 order denying the complaint-dismissal branch of defendant's summary-judgment motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied the branch of defendant's motion seeking summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell because of a broken, downwardly sloped stair at the top of a staircase in defendant's building.

legal_issues.finding: The court required defendant to show its agents/employees did not create the alleged defect and held the overall prima facie showing insufficient; it did not find creation established.

The governing summary-judgment test required absence of actual notice. Defendant failed its overall initial burden; the opinion does not specify which notice evidence was deficient or establish actual notice.

The governing test required absence of constructive notice for sufficient time to discover and remedy the condition. Defendant failed its overall initial burden; constructive notice was not conclusively found.

quality.notes: The short opinion supplies a complete disposition but does not identify specific evidence types or explain the precise evidentiary deficiency. Building subtype, plaintiff's role and accident date are unstated. Stair hazards describe the allegation, not an adjudicated defect.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff commenced the instant action to recover damages for injuries he allegedly sustained when he slipped and fell as a result of a broken, downwardly-sloped stair at the top of a staircase in a building owned by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Jacobson, J.), dated September 11, 2009, which denied that branch of its motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

To demonstrate *881 its entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, the defendant had to establish, prima facie, that its agents or employees neither created the allegedly defective condition that caused the accident, nor had actual or constructive notice of that condition for a sufficient length of time to discover and remedy it
However, the defendant failed to establish its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law

Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied that branch of the defendant’s motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, without regard to the sufficiency of the plaintiffs opposition papers

orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the February 16, 2021 order, limited to summary judgment for the two Macy's defendants.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against Macy's, Inc., and Macy's Corporate Services, Inc.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell on a tomato on the floor of a department store owned and operated by the Macy's defendants on October 30, 2015.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants demonstrated they did not create the alleged condition; plaintiff raised no triable factual issue.
Defendants demonstrated lack of actual notice of the alleged condition; plaintiff raised no triable factual issue.
Defendants demonstrated lack of constructive notice for sufficient time to discover and remedy the condition; plaintiff raised no triable factual issue.

quality.notes: Full affirmance of the appealed branch is binary 0 and favors defendants. The opinion does not identify particular testimony, inspection records or other evidence types supporting the notice showing. Plaintiff's customer/visitor status is unstated; debris is the food item described.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

On October 30, 2015, the plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on a tomato on the floor of a department store owned and operated by the defendants Macy's, Inc., and Macy's Corporate Services, Inc. (hereinafter together the defendants).

The order, insofar as appealed from, granted that branch of the motion of the defendants Macy's, Inc., and Macy's Corporate Services, Inc., which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them.

Here, the defendants established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that they did not create the alleged hazardous condition, or have actual or constructive notice of its existence for a sufficient length of time to have discovered and remedied it
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted that branch of the defendants' motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them.

orders.description: Oster Realty Corp.'s appeal from the September 25, 2014 order denying its summary-judgment motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied Oster's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

facts.factual_summary: Decedent allegedly slipped on ice in front of Food Emporium's grocery store in Oster's shopping center. The opinion locates the fall on a pedestrian ramp between the storefront sidewalk and the adjacent parking lot; the lease's allocation of ramp possession and maintenance was disputed.

legal_issues.finding: Lease provisions governing storefront sidewalks/ramps and common areas did not establish that Oster had transferred all responsibility for the accident area.
Oster failed to address creation in its motion papers, so that alternative basis for summary judgment failed. The court did not find Oster created the ice.
Oster failed to address actual notice in its motion papers; the court did not affirmatively find actual notice.
Oster failed to address constructive notice in its motion papers; the court did not affirmatively find constructive notice.
Oster failed to eliminate triable issues over whether it transferred possession and control of the ramp to Food Emporium; out-of-possession status was not established as a matter of law.

evidence_discussed.description: Oster submitted a lease whose storefront and common-area provisions did not clearly allocate the ramp's possession/control.

quality.notes: The ramp connects a storefront sidewalk to the shopping-center parking lot; it is coded walkway rather than parking_lot. Private shopping-center ownership is supported; the unresolved issue is allocation of control between private owner and tenant, not a stated municipal boundary. The lease sentence split across P002/P003 was read in full; quotations stay within individual passages. Accident date and decedent's role are unstated.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff's decedent allegedly slipped and fell on a patch of ice in front of a grocery store operated by the defendant Food Emporium, Inc. (hereinafter Food Emporium), which rented space in a shopping center owned by the defendant Oster Realty Corp. (hereinafter Oster).

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant Oster Realty Corp. appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Westchester County (Giacomo, J.), dated September 25, 2014, which denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, Oster demonstrated, prima facie, that the decedent slipped and fell on a ramp that descended from a sidewalk in front of Food Emporium's store to an adjacent parking lot controlled by Oster, and not in the parking lot.

However, the copy of the lease submitted by Oster in support of its motion failed to establish, prima facie, that it was an out-of-possession landlord that had transferred possession and control of that ramp to Food Emporium.

Further, pursuant to another lease provision, Oster was responsible for "keeping the common area . . . free of snow [and] ice," and the lease described the "common area" as "all common facilities furnished by [Oster] in the shopping center . . . including but not limited to . . . all access roadways, service roads, ramps, landscaped areas, paved and parking areas within the [*2] shopping center" (emphasis added).

Under these circumstances, Oster failed to establish that there are no triable issues of fact as to whether, pursuant to the lease, it was an out-of-possession landlord that had transferred possession and control of the area where the accident occurred to Food Emporium

Nor did Oster establish its entitlement to summary judgment on the alternative theory that it did not create or have actual or constructive notice of the alleged dangerous condition, since it failed to address those issues in its motion papers
Since Oster failed to make a prima facie showing in support of its motion for summary judgment, the motion was properly denied, regardless of the sufficiency of the opposition papers
We affirm.

orders.description: Appeal from the August 14, 2019 order denying defendant's summary-judgment motion in the home-stairway negligence action.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff, defendant's mother, slipped while descending wooden front-porch steps at defendant's home in October 2015. Testimony described pine needles, moisture and recurring green slime on the steps, as well as a rough handrail; plaintiff said she grabbed railing spindles during her fall.

legal_issues.finding: The court applied the duty to maintain reasonably safe premises; an open and obvious condition does not eliminate that duty.
The court identified noncreation as part of defendant's initial summary-judgment burden. It did not separately find that defendant created a particular defect.
Defendant failed to show absence of actual notice. Her testimony supported a factual question about knowledge of recurring visible slime and failure to correct it.
Defendant failed to establish absence of constructive notice; the court discussed recurring-condition knowledge and testimony about repeated conditions/falls.
The court applied recurring-condition notice principles to evidence of repeated pine needles/slime and earlier falls; liability and notice remained factual questions.
The court held that obviousness does not eliminate the safe-maintenance duty and noted that the possible slimy condition was not always readily observable.
The court considered the speculation rule but found evidence supporting possible structural/slime causes and a contributing handrail condition. It did not conclusively identify a single cause.

Defendant's architect opined that the porch/steps were generally fair to good. Considering the submitted proof, the court nevertheless found defendant's initial showing insufficient; it did not exclude the report.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant submitted her own testimony and plaintiff's deposition about the accident, step conditions, sweeping and complaints.
Family-member testimony described recurring slime/pine needles and a rough handrail.
Defendant submitted color photographs of the porch and wooden steps; the opinion does not independently describe what each photograph depicts.
Architect Leary inspected the porch and steps and supplied an affidavit and report generally assessing them as fair to good.

quality.notes: Private residential control is supported by defendant's home and her maintenance testimony; title ownership is not stated, so defendant_roles is other. Plaintiff's relationship as defendant's mother is explicit but guest/resident status is not. Only October 2015 is given, so accident_date remains null. Pine needles, moisture, slime and handrail defects are allegations/testimony or possible causes, not final findings of liability. Other hazard denotes green slime without inferring its biological identity.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

Plaintiff, who is defendant's mother, commenced this negligence action seeking damages for various injuries that she sustained in October 2015 when she slipped and fell while descending wooden steps attached to a front porch located outside the front door of defendant's home.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court (Lambert, J.), entered August 14, 2019 in Chenango County, which denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

"To prevail on [a] motion for summary judgment, [the] defendant [is] required to establish that its property had been maintained in a reasonably safe condition, and that it did not create a dangerous condition that caused [the] plaintiff's fall or have actual or constructive notice of that condition"
"The fact that a dangerous condition is open and obvious does not relieve [a defendant] of all duty to maintain [his or her] premises in a reasonably safe condition"
"A party who has actual knowledge of an ongoing and recurring dangerous condition can be charged with constructive notice of each specific [recurrence] of that condition"

In support of her motion for summary judgment, defendant offered, among other things, her own testimony, the deposition testimony of plaintiff and several family members, color photographs of the front porch and wooden steps and an affidavit and accompanying report of Daniel Leary, an architect.

Plaintiff explained that, on the morning of the accident, there were a lot of pine needles covering the porch and that it was "dewy" and "misty." Plaintiff acknowledged that she had no difficulty ascending the wooden porch steps but then, when she descended the steps, she slipped on the middle step and fell. After her fall, plaintiff observed pine needles covering the steps where she had fallen. Plaintiff also testified that she grabbed the spindles attached to the railing when she fell to stop herself.

Defendant testified that pine needles made the steps slippery and that, even without the pine needles, the steps are slippery when they are wet and that the steps sometimes appear to be "grimy." Defendant testified that she never treated the wooden porch or steps with water-resistant materials or stain, but she stated that she would regularly sweep the steps to remove the pine needles. Defendant also admitted that both her father and plaintiff complained about the condition of the steps.
Defendant testified that, in addition to plaintiff, several other people have fallen on the same wooden steps, both before and after plaintiff's fall.

Testimony from other witnesses, primarily family members, established that the steps were typically covered in pine needles and often covered in a green substance, which multiple witnesses testified was "slimy." Testimony also established that the handrail was "very rough" and that at least one witness did not use it when she fell for fear that doing so would lead to her being more severely injured.
Leary inspected the subject porch and steps and opined that the "existing conditions and construction of this deck and stair are generally fair to good, and no significant deficiencies are noted."

Based on the foregoing, defendant failed to meet her initial burden of proof demonstrating that the subject step was not a dangerous condition and that she did not have actual or constructive notice of the alleged dangerous condition.

Although plaintiff attributed her fall to pine needles, the foregoing testimony suggests that her fall was likely caused by another defect in the step—whether that be structural or due to the green slimy substance on the step that was not always readily observable

Moreover, the proof submitted by defendant, including her own testimony, demonstrates a question of fact as to whether she had actual notice of the often visible and apparent slimy condition of the step—over and above the pine needles that routinely fell on the step—for a sufficient period of time and that she failed to take corrective action

Also, given witness testimony about concerns regarding the handrail, and viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to plaintiff, Supreme Court properly found that the finder of fact could determine that the condition of the stairway handrail could have contributed to the dangerous condition of the steps and plaintiff's slip and fall
Accordingly, Supreme Court's denial of defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint was proper
"[A] defendant can also demonstrate entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by establishing that the plaintiff cannot identify the cause of his or her fall without engaging in speculation"

orders.description: Appeal, as limited by the briefs, from the order entered on or about May 15, 2019 denying defendants' summary-judgment motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Decedent testified that he tripped over a protruding platform at the base of a product display in defendants' supermarket aisle. The store manager testified that employees erected aisle displays.

legal_issues.finding: The court distinguished a duty to warn from the continuing duty to maintain reasonably safe premises despite an obvious hazard.
Employee assembly of aisle displays permitted a jury to find defendants created the alleged hazard; creation was not conclusively established.
Defendants failed to demonstrate lack of actual notice as part of their summary-judgment showing. The opinion does not separately establish actual notice.
Defendants failed to demonstrate lack of constructive notice as part of their summary-judgment showing. The opinion does not separately establish constructive notice.
The asserted open-and-obvious nature of the condition did not dispose of the safe-maintenance claim; whether the platform was reasonably safe remained a factual issue.
The court recognized that a jury could find the display condition created by defendants was the proximate cause described in decedent's testimony; this remained for the factfinder.

evidence_discussed.description: The court discussed decedent's testimony identifying the display platform as the cause of his trip.
Store manager testimony described employee construction of product displays.

quality.notes: Supermarket aisle and employee erection of displays support private retail control; no title ownership is inferred from the generic owner-duty statement. Decedent's customer/visitor role and accident date are not specified. Limitation by the briefs does not make the affirmance mixed.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Fernando Tapia, J.), entered on or about May 15, 2019, which, as limited by the briefs, denied defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.
Decedent testified that he tripped and fell as a result of a protruding platform at the base of a product display in the aisle of defendants' supermarket.

The court correctly concluded that defendants failed to demonstrate as a matter of law that they did not cause, create, or have actual or constructive notice of the hazardous condition that caused decedent's accident.
The store manager testified that store employees erected product displays in the store aisles.
A jury might find that defendants caused or created the hazardous condition that decedent testified was a proximate cause of his accident
Defendants assert that the condition, if it existed, was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous.

However, an open and obvious hazard may negate the duty to warn, but it does not negate liability in negligence, because an owner still has a duty to ensure that the premises are maintained in a reasonably safe condition
There is an issue of fact as to whether the condition described by decedent was reasonably safe.
